message.content: Industry prices are in an advancing stretch of their cycle rather than at a peak, with prices for chips and for the materials and equipment behind them moving up [D1]. The strongest driver is AI demand that has run beyond the industry's usual planning cycle, leaving procurement needs changing quickly and supply unable to keep pace [D5]. The largest foundry is stepping up equipment purchases in response to that demand [D5]. Labor shortages and infrastructure constraints add to the same strain and affect markets well beyond Taiwan [D5]. Tight supply in parts of the chain is another driver, since mature-node shortages are expected to persist and supply chain management has itself become a lever on pricing [D1]. Cost pressure reinforces it, with materials such as tungsten rising sharply under export restrictions and memory costs pushing chipmakers to shift their product plans [D1]. Capping the advance is capacity expansion, most of all in China, where output has climbed steeply across mature-node chips, memory and packaging [D3]. Tariffs and restrictions between the United States and China cut both ways, raising costs while redirecting where capacity is built [D1]. The wider market is expected to grow strongly, with the AI chip market and geopolitical tension named as the forces that will shape it [D2]. Monthly industry sales have been running above their year-earlier level, which points to demand rather than inventory holding prices up [D4].
